text: You end up describing them. Your Mercury sits on the part of their chart that governs how they show up: their face, their manner, the impression they make before they have said anything. So your talk keeps circling back to them as a subject. You notice how they came across in the meeting. You have a phrase for the way they handle strangers. You tell them what they seemed like before you knew them, and the description usually lands. For them this is a strange mix of flattering and exposing. Most people never say out loud what someone is like. You do, casually, often. If your read is generous they feel seen in a way that steadies them. If it is sharp they carry it around for weeks, because a comment about who a person is does not wash off the way a comment about what they did does. You can usually tell by the moment they go quiet after you have been clever about them. They also tend to talk more around you, and to talk differently. Your company puts them in a verbal mood. They think out loud, try out phrasings, hear themselves. Some of that is genuinely useful, since nobody can see their own manner without a mirror, and you are one. Your side of the exchange is a subject that never runs dry and an audience that responds visibly. You can watch your words change someone's posture in real time. That is rare feedback for a mind that likes to be accurate. It also tempts you to keep going, to refine the portrait past the point where it helps. The useful move is to let your read stay provisional. Say what you notice, then let them correct it. They are the only authority on what it is like to be them, and your description is information, not verdict. Held that way, you become someone they can check themselves against. Held the other way, you become one more voice telling them who they are.

With them, your thinking keeps drifting toward what things cost. Your Mercury falls across the second house of their chart, which holds earnings, belongings, and the private sense of being worth something. You become the one who does the arithmetic out loud. You ask what the rent is. You remember the price of the thing they were considering. You point out that the work pays badly for the hours, or that the old coat is better made than the new one. They experience you as clarifying, and sometimes as intrusive, depending on the week. Numbers are never quite neutral. When you name what something costs, you are also naming what they can and cannot have, and that sits close to how they feel about themselves. A remark you meant as arithmetic can land as an appraisal. You may notice them getting oddly defensive about a purchase you were only curious about. The good version is real, though. Many people never say their finances out loud to anyone, and vagueness there is expensive. You bring language to it. You help them separate what they actually value from what they have simply accumulated, which is a sorting job and therefore yours. Conversations with you tend to end with them knowing what they own and roughly what it is for. Standing here gives your mind solid ground. You like something you can count, and their material life offers a subject with edges on it. There is a quieter benefit too: they treat your practical thinking as valuable, and being useful in a concrete way can matter more to you than being admired. It goes wrong when the commentary never stops, and every choice they make has to pass your appraisal before it is allowed to be a pleasure. What they spend is theirs. The whole exchange improves if you name the number and then let the subject drop.

This is the busiest spot Mercury can land in someone's chart. Your mind arrives in the part of their life that already belongs to talking: their messages, their errands, their reading, the people they grew up alongside, the streets they know by heart. You are meeting them on their own conversational ground, and the result is volume. The two of you will talk more than either of you talks with most people. It shows up as texture rather than depth. Links sent at odd hours. A joke that runs for three years. Half-finished arguments picked up a week later as if no time had passed. You end up knowing their commute, their local grievances, the sibling story, the show they will not stop recommending. Practical information moves between you easily, and it moves fast. They tend to find you easy to reach and easy to think alongside. You match their pace. Where other people need a preamble, you can start in the middle of a sentence and be understood. If they process by talking, you are excellent company. If they do not, your steady stream can feel like weather. In return you get a mind that answers back. Being interested in everything is a lonely trait around people who want a conversation to arrive somewhere. Here it does not have to arrive. You can be curious out loud without justifying it, which is a genuine relief. The risk sits in the same place as the pleasure. Contact this constant can substitute for contact of any other kind, and the two of you can spend years exchanging information without saying anything difficult. There can also be a mild competition over who knows more, who read it first, who is better informed. It stays light, but it is there, and it makes real listening harder than it should be. None of this decides how close the two of you become. It decides that the channel stays open, and that whatever you build gets built out of talk.

You become the one who puts words on their family. Your Mercury sits in the fourth house of their chart, the ground that holds home, ancestry, and the private base a person retreats into. That is not usually a talkative area. Most people carry their childhood as a set of feelings and half-memories nobody has ever described to them. Around you, it gets described. The conversations happen in domestic places: the kitchen, the car, late at night once everyone else has gone. You ask a question about their mother or their grandfather that nobody thought to ask, and the answer surprises both of you. You remember the names in their family and the shape of the old house. Over time you hold a fairly complete map of where they came from, sometimes clearer than the one they hold themselves. For them this can be relief or intrusion, often in the same evening. Naming a family pattern makes it visible, and visible things are harder to keep working around. Some people want exactly that. Others have arranged their peace of mind around not looking, and you will find out which sort they are by how they change the subject. Your side of it is ease. Standing in someone's fourth house means your talk is welcome in their private rooms and not only their public ones. You can think aloud there without arranging yourself first. For a mind used to being the sharp one in company, being merely at home with somebody is worth a great deal. There is a practical side as well. You tend to organize their domestic life whether or not you meant to: the moving plan, the family group chat, the arrangements when something goes wrong at the house. Even at a distance you are often the one keeping the household news in order. A foundation is not only a topic. Talked over too freely, it can unsettle the very thing you were trying to understand.

Your talk lands on their fun. The fifth house covers what a person does for the pleasure of doing it: making things, playing, flirting, betting, the part of life with no purpose beyond enjoyment. With your Mercury sitting there, you become the running commentary on all of it. You are the one they show the draft to. The photo, the demo, the half-written thing gets sent to you, and they want your reaction more than they will admit. You make jokes about the same subject for years and neither of you tires of it. If there are children in their life, you are probably the one who talks to those children like people rather than pets. They tend to be more playful around you and more articulate about what they enjoy. Preferences that were vague get specific. That is Mercury's work, which is sorting. It can also be Mercury's damage, because analysis and play do not always survive each other. If your first response to something they made is an account of how it could be better, you turn a pleasure into homework. Some people quietly stop showing you things and never say why. Here you get an audience for the part of your mind that is not being useful. Wit, wordplay, the show-off register: all of it lands. If your intelligence usually has to justify itself by producing something, this is a spot where it does not. There is a courtship quality to the exchange too, whatever the actual shape of the bond. Attention is being given and enjoyed on purpose. Words are part of the pleasure rather than a means to something else. The thing worth watching is your own timing. Comment while they are making, and you interrupt. Comment after, and you are useful. Most of the trouble here is not what you said but when you said it.

Your mind ends up inside their week. The sixth house is the machinery of a life: the job as it is actually done, the routines, the maintenance, the body's daily upkeep. With your Mercury there, you are the one who notices how their days are assembled, and who says something about it. You spot the inefficiency. You remember the appointment. You point out that they always flag on the same afternoon, that the commute is what ruins Tuesdays, that the system they inherited at work has three steps nobody needs. Much of what you notice is correct, which is both the point and the problem. They tend to get real help from you. Practical intelligence is worth more in this part of life than any other kind, and yours arrives aimed at problems that can actually be solved. Someone who has been vaguely miserable about their schedule for a year can leave one conversation with you holding a fix. That builds a particular sort of trust, based on competence rather than warmth. The cost is that competence in this area shades easily into supervision. Nobody wants a permanent audit of their habits. If every conversation carries a small correction, you turn into the voice in their head saying they are doing it wrong, and that voice does not distinguish between the schedule and the person. Anything touching their health is especially loaded, since a remark there lands close to the body and stays there. The return for you is traction. Some minds are restless without a task, and this arrangement supplies an endless run of small, real problems that respond to attention. There is satisfaction in that which has nothing to do with being thanked. It all works better when they ask. Offered, your sorting is a gift. Volunteered daily, it becomes a job neither of you applied for.

You arrive in their life as a counterpart. The seventh house is where a person meets someone directly: the partner, the client, the opponent, the one across the table. Your Mercury lands there, so they file you under that heading, and the filing happens early. Whatever the bond turns out to be, they deal with you rather than merely knowing you. Conversation between you takes the shape of negotiation, in the neutral sense of the word. Terms get named. You are the one who says what the arrangement actually is, who writes it down, who asks what happens if. Even in an easy friendship the two of you settle small treaties: who pays, who calls, what counts as late. This is not coldness. It is your sorting habit doing its work in the part of their chart that keeps the subject of other people. They tend to think better against you than with you. You are the resistance their reasoning gets to push on. Many people only find out what they believe after arguing it with you once. That makes you valuable and occasionally exhausting, because the same quality that sharpens their thinking will not let a sloppy statement pass. You also become the one they talk to about their other dealings. Their disputes, their contracts, the people they are trying to work out how to handle. You end up holding the file on how they get along with everyone else. In exchange you are taken seriously as an equal. Nobody talks down to a counterpart. Your words carry a weight with them they would not carry had your Mercury landed anywhere else. The trap is treating every conversation as a matter to be settled. Some things between two people are not clauses. Leave a few of them unwritten and the rest of the terms hold better.

You ask them the questions other people leave alone. The eighth house holds what a person keeps off the table: money that is shared or owed, the things done in private, the losses, the parts of a history nobody has been told. Your Mercury lands there, and it does not do small talk in that room. Something about you makes them tell you things. Often they are surprised by it afterward. A fact they had carried alone for years comes out in a conversation neither of you planned, because you asked the plain question in an even tone and did not flinch at the answer. Naming a buried thing changes it. That is the real power in this contact, and power is the right word for it. Practical matters follow the same rule. Where money, property, or obligations are entangled, between the two of you or between them and someone else, you are likely the one who reads the fine print and says the uncomfortable figure out loud. You are also the one who remembers what was owed. For them the experience runs intense and not always comfortable. Being understood at this depth is a relief and a loss of cover at once. Some people pull back hard after telling you too much, and the withdrawal is not really about you. It is about what they can no longer pretend they never said. Your gain is a place where your mind is not spent on the surface. Trivial conversation is a kind of hunger for some people, and there is none of it here. You are also handed material most people never hand over, which counts for something even when it is heavy. What this asks of you is restraint. Knowing where the sore spot is does not mean it needs mentioning. What you do with what you learn matters more than the fact that you learned it.

Their convictions are what the two of you end up arguing about. The ninth house holds the long view: what a person believes, what they think life is for, the places and ideas sitting outside their ordinary range. Your Mercury there puts your thinking directly on their worldview. You question it, usually without meaning to provoke. You ask why they hold that, where it came from, whether it survives the obvious objection. For some people this is the best conversation they have ever had. For others it is an attack on the floor they are standing on. You can generally tell which sort they are within one exchange, though the tell is easy to miss when you are enjoying yourself. The trade runs in an unusual direction here. You give them detail and precision, which their beliefs may have been short of. They give your thinking somewhere to go. Your mind is good with facts and less good at deciding what facts are for, and standing in this part of their chart tends to widen the frame around your own reasoning. Conversations with them are why you started reading in a new area, or booked the trip, or finally studied the thing you had been circling. They come to associate you with the wider world. You are the person who tells them what is happening elsewhere, who recommends the book that changed how they see a subject, who stands for a place or a way of thinking they had no access to before. There is a lecture risk on both sides. Two people can spend years telling each other what life means and never check whether they agree about anything smaller. Big talk is easier than close talk, and it feels more important while it is happening. What holds up over time is the teaching that runs both ways. They stop needing you to agree. You stop needing to win, and the arguments start producing something.

Your remarks about their work carry further than you intend them to. The tenth house is where a person is visible: their career, their standing, the name other people know them by. Your Mercury lands on it, so you become the one who talks about their public life and the one they talk it over with. You draft the message. You suggest the phrasing for the difficult email. You tell them how a decision will look from outside, which is the thing nobody can see for themselves. Over time you may know more about the politics of their workplace than some of their colleagues do, because they think out loud to you about it. Your assessment weighs a great deal with them. A casual comment about their ambition, their boss, or how they came across can lodge for months. That is worth knowing, since you will not always be aiming carefully. What feels to you like a passing observation lands on the part of their life where they are most exposed to judgment, and the two of you may end up with very different memories of how serious the remark was. They may also use you, and mostly not cynically. It is simply convenient to have someone who thinks clearly nearby when a decision about work is due. Being the strategist is a real position, and it can quietly become the whole of what you are to each other if neither of you notices. On your side there is proximity to a life in progress, and often credit of a sort. Your words end up inside their public sentences. Your framing becomes how they explain themselves to their field. For a mind that likes to see its ideas do work in the world, that satisfies, even when nobody knows whose idea it was. The exchange stays healthy while you are still allowed to be no use at all. A counsel who is only ever consulted stops being a person to them.

You land among their people. The eleventh house is the wide circle: friends, the colleagues they chose, the groups they belong to, and the future they hope is coming. Your Mercury there makes you a talker inside their network and not only a talker with them. Introductions come easily. They bring you into rooms, and you are good in those rooms, which reflects well on them. You remember who is connected to whom. You pick up the group's running jokes and its quiet tensions, and you become the one people check things with. Information passes through you, and that position has uses and hazards in equal measure. Much of your actual conversation is about other people and about what comes next. You talk over their plans, the shape they want their life to take in five years, the projects and causes they have attached themselves to. You are good at making a vague hope specific enough to act on. That is a real service, and they will often date a change to a conversation with you. They tend to experience you as a friend before anything else, whatever else the bond becomes. That framing is durable. It survives distance and changes of circumstance, and it keeps the connection from turning possessive, which is not what this part of a chart is built for. Your return is reach. Ideas of yours travel through their circle in a way they would not travel on their own. You also get the ease of company that does not demand intimacy on a schedule. The cost is dilution. A friendship conducted mostly in groups can stay pleasant and thin for years. And being the channel information runs through leaves you one careless sentence from a mess that was never yours. Talk here is cheap to start and expensive to take back.

You put words to things they have never said aloud. The twelfth house is what a person keeps out of view, including from themselves: the private fears, the things that undo them, the hours nobody sees. Your Mercury sits in an area with no natural vocabulary, which makes your presence there strange for both of you. Conversation tends to happen at odd times and in low light. It wanders. It does not resolve. The two of you will talk about something for an hour and afterward be unable to say what it was, only that it mattered. Now and then you say the exact sentence they needed and did not know existed, and they keep it for years. Practical communication is the weak spot. Messages go astray here. Details get lost, plans are misremembered, one of you is certain a thing was agreed and the other has no record of it. This is not carelessness on either side. Your ordinary sorting function is working in the part of their chart where things dissolve, and it operates less crisply there than anywhere else. They may also find you hard to place. You can occupy an important position in their inner life while being nearly invisible in the rest of it, unmentioned to their friends, filed under no category at all. That can feel peaceful or lonely depending on what you were hoping for. The gift, when it goes well, is unguarded speech. No performance is required. You can think in half-sentences and be followed. That is rare for a mind that usually has to be sharp before anyone listens. What it asks is patience with vagueness and honesty about the gaps. Plans do better written down. The quiet thing does better said while it is still small. Most of what goes wrong between you goes wrong through silence rather than conflict.
